notes.front: What is an artifact in Scrum, in one sentence?
notes.back: One of Scrum’s three formal records, representing work or value, designed to maximise transparency.
notes.explanation: Everyone inspecting an artifact has the same basis for adaptation.
notes.example: Like a scoreboard: it shows everyone the same state of play.

notes.front: What is an artifact’s commitment in Scrum, in one sentence?
notes.back: The goal or standard each artifact contains, against which progress can be measured.
notes.explanation: Commitments exist to reinforce empiricism; each makes sure its artifact gives information that enhances transparency and focus.
notes.example: Like the finish line on a race track: it tells you how far you still have to go.

notes.front: What is the Product Backlog, in one sentence?
notes.back: An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product; the Scrum Team’s single source of work.
notes.explanation: Emergent means it keeps developing as more is learned; ordered means its items are arranged in a sequence.
notes.example: Like one to-do list for a house renovation, kept in order and rewritten as you discover what the walls hide.

notes.front: What is the Product Goal, in one sentence?
notes.back: A future state of the product that the Scrum Team plans against: its long-term objective.
notes.explanation: It sits in the Product Backlog, and the rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define what will fulfil it.
notes.example: Like “a café that can serve 200 lunches a day”, which every task on the renovation list serves.

notes.front: What is the Sprint Goal, in one sentence?
notes.back: The single objective for a Sprint.
notes.explanation: It gives focus and coherence, while leaving flexibility in the exact work needed to reach it.
notes.example: Like “customers can pay by card”, rather than a list of ten unrelated tasks.

notes.front: What is the Sprint Backlog, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Developers’ plan for the Sprint: the Sprint Goal (why), the selected Product Backlog items (what), and how to deliver them.
notes.explanation: It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the Sprint’s work, updated as more is learned.
notes.example: Like a trip itinerary: why you are going, the places chosen, and the day-by-day route, adjusted as you go.

notes.front: What is an Increment, in one sentence?
notes.back: A concrete, usable stepping stone toward the Product Goal, adding to all earlier Increments.
notes.explanation: Each Increment is thoroughly verified so that all Increments work together; to provide value, it must be usable.
notes.example: Like adding a finished room to a house: usable now, and part of the whole.

notes.front: What is the Definition of Done, in one sentence?
notes.back: A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product.
notes.explanation: It gives everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.
notes.example: Like a pilot’s pre-flight checklist: until every item is ticked, the plane is not ready.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: What is Product Backlog refinement, in one sentence?
notes.back: Breaking Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items, and adding detail such as description, order and size.
notes.explanation: It is ongoing, and it is how items usually become clear enough to be selected for a Sprint.
notes.example: Like turning “fix up the kitchen” into “replace the tap”, “tile the wall” and “fit the shelves”.

notes.front: How many artifacts does Scrum have, and what are they?
notes.back: Three: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment.
notes.explanation: Each one contains a commitment: the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done.

notes.front: The Product Backlog’s commitment is the {{c1::Product Goal}}.
notes.explanation: The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog; the rest of the Product Backlog defines what will fulfil it.

notes.front: The Sprint Backlog’s commitment is the {{c1::Sprint Goal}}.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Goal is the “why” of the Sprint Backlog.

notes.front: The Increment’s commitment is the {{c1::Definition of Done}}.
notes.explanation: Work is part of an Increment only once it meets the Definition of Done.

notes.front: How many Product Goals does a Scrum Team work toward at a time?
notes.back: One. It must fulfil or abandon one before taking on the next.
notes.explanation: The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team.

notes.front: Who is responsible for sizing Product Backlog items?
notes.back: The Developers who will be doing the work.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner may influence them by helping them understand and select trade-offs.

notes.front: When is a Product Backlog item ready to be selected for a Sprint?
notes.back: When the Scrum Team can get it Done within one Sprint.
notes.explanation: Items usually reach this degree of transparency through refinement.

notes.front: Who is the Sprint Backlog by and for?
notes.back: The Developers.
notes.explanation: It should have enough detail for them to inspect their progress each day.

notes.front: When is an Increment born?
notes.back: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: Work cannot be considered part of an Increment until it meets the Definition of Done.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: What happens to a Product Backlog item that does not meet the Definition of Done?
notes.back: It cannot be released or presented; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
notes.explanation: There is no “partly done” Increment.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: Can more than one Increment be created within a Sprint?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint, and each is additive to all prior Increments.

notes.front: If the organisation has a Definition of Done as a standard, what must its Scrum Teams do?
notes.back: Follow it as a minimum.
notes.explanation: If there is no organisational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: Several Scrum Teams work on the same product. How many Definitions of Done do they use?
notes.back: One: they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Definition of Done gives everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: A feature is built but untested, and the Definition of Done requires testing. The Sprint ends tomorrow. Can it count as part of the Increment?
notes.back: No. Work is part of an Increment only once it meets the Definition of Done.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the Product Owner agrees
B) No, it must meet the Definition of Done
C) Yes, marked as partly done
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done; a Product Owner’s agreement does not change that. C: an item that does not meet it returns to the Product Backlog instead.
notes.explanation: The Definition of Done is the Increment’s commitment: the standard it is measured against.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: A team delivers a usable, Done feature to customers on day 6 of a 14-day Sprint. Is that allowed?
notes.back: Yes. An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends.
notes.explanation: Scrum does not make teams hold back finished, usable work until the Sprint is over.

notes.front: Is a burn-down chart one of Scrum’s artifacts?
notes.back: No. The three artifacts are the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog and the Increment.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide mentions burn-downs only as one of various practices for forecasting progress, which do not replace empiricism.

notes.front: A backlog has 400 items and no order at all. Which property of a Product Backlog is missing?
notes.back: Order: the Product Backlog is an ordered list.
notes.explanation: Ordering the Product Backlog is part of the Product Owner’s accountability.

notes.front: Which artifact is this: the objective, the chosen items and the plan for the current Sprint?
notes.back: The Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: Why (the Sprint Goal), what (the selected items) and how (the plan) together make the Sprint Backlog.

notes.front: A team’s goal is “our booking service is live in every region within two years”. Is that a Sprint Goal or a Product Goal?
notes.back: A Product Goal: a long-term future state of the product.
notes.explanation: A Sprint Goal is the single objective for one Sprint of a month or less.

notes.front: A proposed Sprint Goal is “finish tickets 14, 15 and 22”. Does it leave the flexibility a Sprint Goal should?
notes.back: No. It fixes the exact work, while a Sprint Goal is a single objective that leaves flexibility in the exact work needed.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide says the Sprint Goal provides flexibility in terms of the exact work needed to achieve it, and creates coherence and focus.

notes.front: The team splits “improve search” into three smaller items and gives each a size. What activity is this?
notes.back: Product Backlog refinement.
notes.explanation: Refinement breaks items down and adds detail such as description, order and size.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog?
notes.back: Product Backlog: everything needed to improve the product. Sprint Backlog: the Developers’ plan for the current Sprint.
notes.explanation: Items are selected from the Product Backlog into the Sprint Backlog.
notes.contrast: Whole product, ordered by the Product Owner, versus one Sprint, planned by the Developers.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Product Goal and the Sprint Goal?
notes.back: Product Goal: the long-term objective for the product. Sprint Goal: the single objective for one Sprint.
notes.explanation: Sprints are steps toward the Product Goal.
notes.contrast: Long-term and product-wide versus one Sprint.
